knowledgeNodes.name: Simple Event in Probability
knowledgeNodes.definition: An event that consists of exactly one outcome from the sample space.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe how probabilities are used to represent the likelihood of a result of an experiment ... and the likelihood of a real-world event

knowledgeNodes.name: Compound Event in Probability
knowledgeNodes.definition: An event that consists of two or more simple events.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive, and solve related probability problems

knowledgeNodes.name: Subset in Probability Context
knowledgeNodes.definition: A set whose elements are all contained within a larger set (the sample space or another event).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: describe a sample space as a set that contains all possible outcomes of an experiment, and distinguish between a discrete sample space ... and a continuous sample space

knowledgeNodes.name: Intersection of Sets
knowledgeNodes.definition: The set of elements that belong to both set A and set B, denoted A ∩ B.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe an event ... determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive, and solve related probability problems

knowledgeNodes.name: Union of Sets
knowledgeNodes.definition: The set of elements that belong to either set A or set B (or both), denoted A ∪ B.

knowledgeNodes.name: Disjoint (Mutually Exclusive) Sets
knowledgeNodes.definition: Two sets with no common elements; their intersection is the empty set.

knowledgeNodes.name: Union Size Formula
knowledgeNodes.definition: For two sets, the number of elements in their union is given by |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|.

knowledgeNodes.name: Three-Set Venn Diagram Procedure
knowledgeNodes.definition: Step-by-step method: 1) Fill triple intersection, 2) Subtract triple from each two-set intersection to get two-set-only values, 3) Subtract overlapping segments from each set total to get single-set-only values, 4) Verify totals.

knowledgeNodes.name: Theoretical Probability Calculation
knowledgeNodes.definition: Probability of an event = number of outcomes in the event divided by total number of outcomes in the sample space (all equally likely).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: determine the theoretical probability, Pi, of each outcome of a discrete sample space, recognize that the sum of the probabilities is 1, and solve related problems

reteachModules.trigger: Student starts filling Venn diagram from single-set regions or gives incorrect procedure in describing the steps.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes they can fill the single-set (only one sport) regions first, not realizing that the triple intersection must be placed before the two-set or single-set regions to avoid overlapping errors.

miniLesson.explain: When constructing a three-set Venn diagram, always begin by filling in the number of elements that belong to all three sets (the triple intersection). Then subtract that number from the given two-set intersections to get the values for exactly two sets. Finally, subtract the overlapping parts from each set total to get the number that belong to exactly one set. This order ensures correct totals.
miniLesson.example: In the three-sport example: volleyball=15, basketball=12, swimming=10, triple intersection=3, basketball&swimming=4, volleyball&swimming=4, volleyball&basketball=8. Start by placing 3 in the center. Then for volleyball&basketball but not swimming: 8 - 3 = 5. Similarly, basketball&swimming only: 4 - 3 = 1, volleyball&swimming only: 4 - 3 = 1. Then for only volleyball: 15 - (5+3+1) = 6, only basketball: 12 - (5+3+1) = 3, only swimming: 10 - (1+3+1) = 5. Total: 6+5+3+1+1+3+5 = 24, verifying totals.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: TRIple first: T for Triple, R for Region, I for Intersection. Always start with the center (triple intersection) of the Venn diagram.

After placing the triple intersection (3) in a three-sport Venn diagram, what number goes in the region 'volleyball and basketball, but not swimming'? (Hint: given volleyball&basketball=8)

reteachModules.trigger: Student confuses 'and' (intersection) with 'or' (union) in probability problems.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student does not distinguish between the intersection (AND) and union (OR) of events. They may think 'and' means adding probabilities together, or they confuse the two terms in word problems, resulting in incorrect operations.

miniLesson.explain: In probability, 'and' refers to the intersection (overlap) of two events, while 'or' refers to the union (all outcomes in either event). For events A and B: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). This formula subtracts the overlap to avoid double-counting. If A and B are mutually exclusive (disjoint), P(A and B)=0, so P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B).
miniLesson.example: In a three-sport example with 24 total students: 15 play volleyball (V), 12 play basketball (B), 8 play both. P(V and B)=8/24=1/3. P(V or B)=(15+12-8)/24=19/24. Notice the union is larger and subtracts the overlap.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: 'AND' = small overlap (intersection); 'OR' = big combined set minus the double-counted middle.

reteachModules.trigger: Student adds set totals without subtracting the intersection when finding the union.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student thinks that the number of elements in the union is simply the sum of the elements in each set, not realizing that overlapping elements are counted twice.

miniLesson.explain: When finding the union of two sets (A ∪ B), you must add the number of elements in each set and then subtract the number of elements that are in both sets (the intersection). This is because those overlapping elements are counted twice if you just add. The formula is |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|.
miniLesson.example: In a sports club, 18 students play volleyball, 20 play basketball, and 13 play both. To find how many play volleyball or basketball, do: 18 + 20 - 13 = 25. Simply adding 18+20=38 would double-count the 13 who play both.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Don't double-count the overlap; subtract the intersection.

reteachModules.trigger: It looks like the Venn diagram totals weren't checked. Always verify each set's total after filling all regions.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student thinks that after filling in the numbers from the given data, the region values are automatically correct without needing to sum them back to the original set totals.

miniLesson.explain: After filling all regions in a Venn diagram, you must verify that the sum of regions for each set equals the given total for that set. This catches arithmetic or logic errors, such as forgetting to subtract the triple intersection from a two-set overlap.
miniLesson.example: Three-sport example: volleyball=15, basketball=12, swimming=10, triple=3, basketball&swimming=4, volleyball&swimming=4, volleyball&basketball=8. Correct filling: triple=3; basketball&swimming only=4-3=1; volleyball&swimming only=4-3=1; volleyball&basketball only=8-3=5; volleyball only=15-(5+3+1)=6; basketball only=12-(5+3+1)=3; swimming only=10-(1+3+1)=5. Verification: volleyball total=6+5+3+1=15; basketball total=3+5+1+3=12; swimming total=5+1+1+3=10. All match. If you skipped verification, you might think the numbers are correct when they aren't.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Verify totals: After filling, check each set's sum against the original total. If sums don't match, go back and adjust.

guidedPractice.prompt: In a survey, 18 students play volleyball, 20 play basketball, and 13 play both. The Venn diagram has been filled with: only volleyball = 5, only basketball = 7, both = 13, neither = 0. Verify if the totals match. Show your work.
guidedPractice.answer: Volleyball total = only volleyball + both = 5 + 13 = 18, matches given total of 18. Basketball total = only basketball + both = 7 + 13 = 20, matches given total of 20. Both is given as 13, which matches. The neither region is consistent (0). Therefore, the diagram is verified correctly.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student filled a three-set Venn diagram for volleyball (15), basketball (12), swimming (10), triple intersection = 3, with the following region values: volleyball & basketball only = 8, volleyball & swimming only = 4, basketball & swimming only = 4, volleyball only = 0, basketball only = 0, swimming only = 0. Use verification to find the error(s).
guidedPractice.answer: Check volleyball total: 0 + 8 + 4 + 3 = 15, matches given 15. Check basketball total: 0 + 8 + 4 + 3 = 15, but given total is 12. There is an error: volleyball & basketball only should be 8 - 3 = 5, not 8. Similarly, check swimming: 0 + 4 + 4 + 3 = 11, but given total is 10. Error: volleyball & swimming only should be 4 - 3 = 1, and basketball & swimming only should be 4 - 3 = 1. The student did not subtract the triple intersection from the two-set intersections. Correct the triple intersection is subtracted: v&b only = 8-3=5, v&s only = 4-3=1, b&s only = 4-3=1. Then recompute: volleyball only = 15 - (5+3+1) = 6, basketball only = 12 - (5+3+1) = 3, swimming only = 10 - (1+3+1) = 5. After correction, totals verify: volleyball = 6+5+3+1=15, basketball = 3+5+1+3=12, swimming = 5+1+1+3=10.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain why verification is important after filling a Venn diagram. Provide a step-by-step verification process for the three-sport example: volleyball=15, basketball=12, swimming=10, triple=3, v&b=8, v&s=4, b&s=4, total students=24.
guidedPractice.answer: Verification is important because it catches arithmetic mistakes and ensures that all regions are correctly derived from the given totals. Without verification, errors like forgetting to subtract the triple intersection may go undetected. Step-by-step verification for the three-sport example: 1. Fill the triple intersection: 3. 2. For each two-set intersection, subtract the triple to get the two-set-only values: v&b only = 8-3=5, v&s only = 4-3=1, b&s only = 4-3=1. 3. For each set, subtract the sum of overlapping regions (including triple) from the given total to get the only region: volleyball only = 15 - (5+3+1) = 6; basketball only = 12 - (5+3+1) = 3; swimming only = 10 - (1+3+1) = 5. 4. Verify each set total by adding its only region plus all overlapping regions: volleyball total = 6+5+1+3 = 15 (matches given 15); basketball total = 3+5+1+3 = 12 (matches 12); swimming total = 5+1+1+3 = 10 (matches 10). 5. Optionally, verify total students by summing all regions: 6+3+5+5+1+1+3 = 24 (matches total). If any check fails, recheck calculations from step 1.

cards.question: When rolling a fair 20-sided die, which of the following is a simple event?
options: Rolling a number greater than 15
Rolling a 7
Rolling a number divisible by 5
Rolling an odd number
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of simple vs compound event.
misconceptions: That event contains multiple outcomes (16,17,18,19,20), so it is compound.
✓ Correct. A simple event has exactly one outcome, such as rolling a 7.
That event contains four outcomes (5,10,15,20), so it is compound.
That event contains ten outcomes, so it is compound.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies that a simple event has exactly one outcome.
cards.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe how probabilities are used to represent the likelihood of a result of an experiment (e.g., spinning spinners; drawing tokens from a bag with replacement; tossing a coin) and the likelihood of a real-world event (e.g., that it will rain tomorrow, that an accident will occur when crossing an intersection, that there will be a power failure)
cards.alignmentNote: officialExpectationCode A1.1 matches the knowledge node, but node_id is null in the bank.
cards.commonMisconception: Thinking 'rolling an even number' is a simple event because it feels simple.

cards.question: In the sports club example (18 volleyball, 20 basketball, 13 both), which event is 'plays volleyball OR basketball'?
options: 13 students
25 students
38 students
15 students
cards.diagnosis: Test understanding of union ('or') vs intersection ('and').
misconceptions: 13 is the number who play both (intersection), not the union.
✓ Correct. Union = 18 + 20 - 13 = 25.
You added without subtracting the overlap. The correct union is 25.
15 is not a value from this data. Check your calculation.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly interprets union (OR) and uses formula to find 25.
cards.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive (e.g., the events of getting an even number or getting an odd number of heads from tossing a coin 5 times are mutually exclusive), and solve related probability problems [e.g., calculate P(~A), P(A and B), P(A or B)] using a variety of strategies (e.g., Venn diagrams, lists, formulas)
cards.alignmentNote: A1.5 covers union/intersection and probability problems.
cards.commonMisconception: Adding 18+20=38 without subtracting overlap, or confusing 'and' (13) with 'or'.

cards.question: In a class, 12 students play basketball, 15 play volleyball, and 5 play both. How many students play basketball or volleyball?
cards.diagnosis: Check ability to use union formula without overcounting.
misconceptions: You added without subtracting the 5 who play both. The formula is |A|+|B|-|A∩B|.
5 is the number who play both, not the union.
This might come from guessing. Use the union formula.
cards.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive (e.g., the events of getting an even number or getting an odd number of heads from tossing a coin 5 times are mutually exclusive), and solve related probability problems [e.g., calculate P(~A), P(A and B), P(A or B)] using a variety of strategies (e.g., Venn diagrams, lists, formulas)
cards.commonMisconception: Simply adding |A|+|B| = 27 without subtracting the overlap.

cards.question: When filling a three-set Venn diagram for volleyball (15), basketball (12), swimming (10), triple intersection = 3, basketball & swimming = 4, volleyball & swimming = 4, volleyball & basketball = 8, what should you fill first?
options: The value for students who play only volleyball.
The value for students who play all three sports.
The value for students who play volleyball and basketball but not swimming.
The total number of students.
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of correct order in Venn diagram construction.
misconceptions: Starting with single-set values often leads to errors. Always begin with the triple intersection.
✓ Correct. Always start with the triple intersection, then adjust two-set intersections and single-set values.
That is a two-set-only value, which should be filled after the triple intersection.
The total is used at the end to verify, not to start filling.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies that the triple intersection must be placed first.
cards.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive (e.g., the events of getting an even number or getting an odd number of heads from tossing a coin 5 times are mutually exclusive), and solve related probability problems [e.g., calculate P(~A), P(A and B), P(A or B)] using a variety of strategies (e.g., Venn diagrams, lists, formulas)
cards.alignmentNote: Venn diagram procedure is part of solving probability problems in A1.5.
cards.commonMisconception: Starting with single-set (only volleyball) instead of triple intersection.

cards.question: Using the three-sport Venn diagram from earlier (total 24 students), what is the probability that a randomly selected student plays volleyball?
cards.diagnosis: Check ability to compute probability from Venn diagram data and verify set totals.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. Volleyball total is 15 out of 24 students.
That is the probability for basketball, not volleyball.
8 is the number who play both volleyball and basketball, not total volleyball.
3 is the triple intersection, not total volleyball.
cards.successCriteria: Student calculates P(volleyball) = 15/24 = 5/8 correctly by reading from correctly filled diagram.
cards.ossdExpectation: determine the theoretical probability, P, of each outcome of a discrete sample space (e.g., P(heads) = 1/2, P(rolling a 6) = 1/6), recognize that the sum of the probabilities is 1, and solve related problems
cards.alignmentNote: Probability calculation from Venn diagram aligns with A1.3.
cards.commonMisconception: Using the total volleyball number from the problem statement (15) but not verifying that the diagram regions sum to 15, leading to undetected errors.

cards.question: Two events are mutually exclusive (disjoint) if:
options: They can happen at the same time.
Their intersection is the empty set.
Their union is the sample space.
They have the same probability.
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of disjoint sets and relation to intersection.
misconceptions: Mutually exclusive means they cannot happen simultaneously.
✓ Correct. Disjoint sets have no common elements, so P(A and B) = 0.
That would be exhaustive, not necessarily disjoint.
Probability equality is not related to being disjoint.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly defines disjoint sets as having no common outcomes.
cards.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive (e.g., the events of getting an even number or getting an odd number of heads from tossing a coin 5 times are mutually exclusive), and solve related probability problems [e.g., calculate P(~A), P(A and B), P(A or B)] using a variety of strategies (e.g., Venn diagrams, lists, formulas)
